title: The Peak-End Rule

scenes.vo: In one experiment, people chose to go through more pain. Here's why.

scenes.text:
Trial 1: hand in cold water
for *60 seconds*
scenes.vo: Participants held a hand in painfully cold water for 60 seconds.

scenes.text:
Trial 2: the same 60 sec…
+ *30 sec* slightly less cold
scenes.vo: In another trial, they did the same 60 seconds, plus 30 more where the water got slightly warmer.

scenes.text:
Which would you repeat?
*Most* chose the longer one
scenes.vo: When asked which trial they'd repeat, most chose the longer one. More total pain, but a better ending.
We don't remember how long an experience lasted. We remember its most intense moment and how it ended.
This is the peak-end rule. It's why a great last day saves a so-so holiday, and a rude goodbye ruins a good meal.

scenes.text: End things well. The last moment *writes the memory*.
scenes.vo: So end things well: meetings, dates, presentations. The last moment writes the memory.

scenes.text:
Follow *@inquisitive_bytes*
for a daily byte of behaviour science
scenes.vo: Follow Inquisitive Bytes for a daily byte of behaviour science.

caption:
Your memory isn't a recording. It's a highlight reel of the peak and the ending. 🎬

What's an experience that a great (or terrible) ending completely changed? 👇
source: Kahneman, D., Fredrickson, B. L., Schreiber, C. A. & Redelmeier, D. A. (1993). When more pain is preferred to less: Adding a better end. Psychological Science, 4(6).
